newsitem.title: USA: US bonds looking at data, barely notice dlr drop.
newsitem.headline: US bonds looking at data, barely notice dlr drop.

text.p: In a sharp contrast to usual protocol, the dollar's dramatic drop against the yen during the past couple of sessions has had little impact on the U.S. Treasury market.

Rather, Treasuries have improved, as analysts said the market is more concerned over the outlook for the U.S. economy and Federal Reserve policy. Players noted that odds of a rate hike on May 20 have fallen to below 50-50 on news the economy may be starting to moderate.

On Monday, the 30-year bond's yield was down five basis points and the two-year note was down 11 basis points since Thursday's close. Meanwhile, the dollar was at 119.30 yen, down from 123.62 late Thursday and 125 yen at Wednesday's close.

"I don't get the sense of a crisis," said Dan Seto, senior economist at Nikko Securities Co. "The dollar made a big move, but unless it kicks down to 115 (yen) you won't see investors panicking over fluctuations."
The fact Treasuries have done so well in the wake of the dollar's drop has both surprised and pleased the market.
"In the old days, we would have been crushed," said a head bond trader at a large U.S. primary dealership. "But it shows the cycle is OK since Treasuries held in."
Traders reported only minor selling of Treausries by Japanese investors as the dollar dove.
"Whatever Japan sold, Asia bought three times that much," said Vincent Verterano, head trader at Nomura Securities International Inc. "Demand is coming from other parts of the world."
Talk has circulated in the market in recent sessions of heavy buying by investors and central banks in China and Thailand.

"There are some other forces at large, more powerful than Japanese selling," noted a head trader at a U.S. bank/dealer. "Japan is not as big a percentage of investors out there. They are still a powerful force, but not as much as five or six years ago."
According to the Treasury, Japan is still the largest foreign holder of U.S. Treasuries, accounting for 8.5 percent, followed by the U.K. at about 6.0 percent.
Foreign holdings were nearly 35 percent at the end of February, up from 32 percent at the end of 1996.

The trader said that he has not seen any heavy selling based on the dollar's move, even from Japan. "We have seen activity, but no major liquidations," he said. "I think you will need a rise of 50 to 70 basis points (in Japanese rates) before getting people to think about moving out of the U.S. into JGBs."
Indeed, market participants said that even with the big downward move in the dollar, many factors weigh in favor of continued solid demand for U.S. Treasuries.

"The dollar was reflecting a healthy retracement," said Paul Roberti," senior salesman at Yamaichi International (America) Inc. "We still have a strong economy with low inflation and are in the early stages of having a budget under control. There is not another country you could say that about."

One factor in favor of continued investment in U.S. Treasuries is a 400-basis-point spread between Treasuries and equivelant Japanese government bonds. And despite an improving Japanese economy, it is still unlikely the Bank of Japan will hike interest rates rates, analysts said.

Roberti and most other players said the Treasury market is too concerned about U.S. economic data to worry about what the Japanese reponse will be from a fall in the dollar. Some noted that the positive tone reflects an expectation of bond-friendly data this week and lessening odds of a tightening by the Federal Reserve later this month.

The dollar started heading south after comments from senior Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara on Thursday saying the dollar could fall as low as 103 yen based on historical moves in dollar/yen.

The dollar was further beat-up on Friday on a combination of more jawboning from Japanese officials, fears of coordinated intervention against the dollar, improving odds of higher Japanese rates and waning odds of higher U.S. rates.
Fred Sturm, first vice president of futures and options at Fuji Securities, said he expects the dollar to weaken further. That, he said, will lead to unloading of Treasuries by central banks.
"Sometime, in the next few days, we will see central bank selling," he said. "And then (Treasury market investors) will say, "geez, get me out."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
